slide 4 ('What Is Spec-Driven Development?'): [fact] The notes claim that spec-driven development eliminates the gap where documentation diverges from actual API behavior, which is an overstatement because specifications can still drift from implementations unless conformance is continuously validated. Fix: Say that spec-driven development reduces documentation drift by making the specification authoritative and by validating implementations against it. (rewritten to fix this; not re-read by the reviewer)

slide 5 ('Core Principles of SDD'): [fact] The claim that contracts are expressed in neutral formats such as YAML, JSON, and Protobuf so any language or tool can consume them is misleading because Protobuf is a language-specific interface-definition mechanism and the listed formats do not make every contract tool-compatible. Fix: Say that contracts use structured, machine-readable formats such as YAML or JSON, while framework-specific formats such as Protobuf are used where their type system and tooling are appropriate. (found before the rewrite; the slide may have moved)

slide 6 ('Major Spec‑Driven Frameworks'): [fact] Calling OpenAPI, GraphQL SDL, Protocol Buffers, and AsyncAPI all "spec-driven frameworks" conflates specification formats and schemas with development frameworks that generate code and enforce contracts. Fix: Describe these as widely used API specification formats or contract-definition technologies used within spec-driven development. (found before the rewrite; the slide may have moved)

slide 8 ('GraphQL Schema Definition Language'): [fact] The bullet "Directives for auth & caching" is misleading because GraphQL SDL has no built-in standard directives for authentication or caching; @auth is not a standard GraphQL directive. Fix: Say that custom directives can carry application metadata such as authorization hints or caching policy, while @deprecated is a built-in directive. (rewritten to fix this; not re-read by the reviewer)

slide 8 ('GraphQL Schema Definition Language'): [fact] The statement that introspection is enabled by default is not universally true because GraphQL servers may disable or restrict introspection in production. Fix: Say that introspection is commonly enabled by default in development and can be disabled or restricted in production. (found before the rewrite; the slide may have moved)

slide 9 ('Protocol Buffers (proto3)'): [fact] The claim that Protobuf field numbers provide forward and backward compatibility is too broad because compatibility depends on correct field-number management and valid wire changes. Fix: Say that stable field numbers and compatible wire-format changes support backward and forward compatibility. (found before the rewrite; the slide may have moved)

slide 9 ('Protocol Buffers (proto3)'): [fact] The statement that the Protobuf binary encoding is smaller and faster than JSON is not universally true because relative size and performance depend on the data and implementation. Fix: Say that Protobuf's compact binary encoding is often smaller and faster to parse than equivalent JSON representations. (found before the rewrite; the slide may have moved)

slide 11 ('Worked Example: User Login API'): [code] The OpenAPI snippet uses `format: password`, which is not a standard OpenAPI 3.1 format and may be rejected by strict validators. Fix: Remove `format: password` and describe the password field with `type: string`, optionally adding `writeOnly: true` and an appropriate length or pattern constraint. (rewritten to fix this; not re-read by the reviewer)

slide 11 ('Worked Example: User Login API'): [fact] The notes describe the access token as JWT-style, but the schema does not constrain or document the token format, so the example does not establish that property. Fix: Either describe the token as an opaque access token or add a description stating that it is a JWT. (found before the rewrite; the slide may have moved)

slide 13 ('Executable Specifications & Contract Testing'): [fact] The bullet "Prevents breaking changes" overstates what consumer-driven contract testing guarantees because it detects incompatible changes but does not prevent them from being introduced or merged. Fix: Say that consumer-driven contract testing detects breaking changes before deployment. (found before the rewrite; the slide may have moved)

slide 14 ('Ensuring Interface Conformance at Runtime'): [fact] The bullet "Schema validation libraries (ajv, protoc)" incorrectly presents protoc as a schema-validation library; protoc is the Protocol Buffers compiler, while ajv validates JSON Schema. Fix: List ajv as a JSON Schema validator and describe protoc separately as the Protocol Buffers compiler and code-generation entry point. (rewritten to fix this; not re-read by the reviewer)

slide 14 ('Ensuring Interface Conformance at Runtime'): [fact] The notes say that code generators produce router skeletons that enforce the spec, but generated skeletons generally do not enforce request and response schemas by themselves. Fix: Say that generated code provides typed routes and models, while separate validation middleware or generated validation hooks enforce the contract. (found before the rewrite; the slide may have moved)

slide 14 ('Ensuring Interface Conformance at Runtime'): [fact] The notes describe Schemathesis and Dredd as property-based test generators, but they are primarily API testing tools that derive test cases from an API description rather than general property-based generators. Fix: Describe Schemathesis and Dredd as tools that generate and run API tests from an OpenAPI description. (found before the rewrite; the slide may have moved)

slide 17 ('Key Takeaways'): [fact] The takeaway "Contract testing guarantees conformance across services" overstates the guarantee because contract tests cover only the interactions and rules encoded in the contracts. Fix: Say that contract testing helps detect conformance regressions across service boundaries. (found before the rewrite; the slide may have moved)

slide 18 ('Lab Preview: Executable Specification Lab'): [other] The lab preview combines OpenAPI stub generation with a Pact contract test suite without explaining how the Pact contract relates to the OpenAPI document, which may confuse students about which artifact is under test. Fix: State whether students will derive Pact contracts from the OpenAPI document or author them separately, and identify which artifact each test validates. (found before the rewrite; the slide may have moved)
